stem: A set of straight, parallel wavefronts travels across a shallow-water tank. Which statement correctly describes a ray representing the wave?
options: The ray is perpendicular to each wavefront.
The ray lies along a wavefront.
The ray represents the motion of an individual water molecule.
The ray always points towards the source.
explanation: A ray indicates the direction of energy propagation and is normal to each wavefront.
sourceNote: Original item aligned to IB Physics guide for first assessment 2025, and benchmarked against the supplied C.3 Paper 1A questions.

stem: A plane wavefront meets a straight reflecting barrier at an angle of incidence of 35° measured from the normal. What is the angle between the reflected ray and the normal?
explanation: The angle of reflection equals the angle of incidence, both measured from the normal.
sourceNote: Original item aligned to IB Physics guide for first assessment 2025, and benchmarked against the supplied C.3 Paper 1A questions.

stem: Water waves travel from deep water into shallow water. Their speed decreases by 25% while the source frequency is unchanged. What happens to their wavelength?
options: It becomes 1.33 times larger.
It stays unchanged.
It becomes 0.75 of its original value.
It becomes 0.25 of its original value.
explanation: v = fλ; unchanged f means the wavelength changes in the same proportion as wave speed.
sourceNote: Original item aligned to IB Physics guide for first assessment 2025, and benchmarked against the supplied C.3 Paper 1A questions.

stem: A light ray passes from medium 1 into medium 2 as shown. The incident angle is 45° and the refracted angle is 28°. Which statement is correct?
options: The speed of light in medium 2 is greater than in medium 1.
The refractive index of medium 2 is smaller than that of medium 1.
The frequency of the light decreases at the boundary.
The speed of light in medium 2 is less than in medium 1.
explanation: The ray bends towards the normal, implying higher refractive index and lower speed in medium 2. Frequency is constant.
diagramAlt: A ray passes from medium 1 into medium 2, bending towards the normal, with angles of 45 degrees and 28 degrees.
sourceNote: Original item aligned to IB Physics guide for first assessment 2025, and benchmarked against the supplied C.3 Paper 1A questions.

stem: The critical angle for a glass–air boundary is 42°. A ray inside the glass meets the boundary at 50° to the normal. What happens?
options: The ray is totally internally reflected.
The ray is refracted at 50° to the normal.
The ray exits along the boundary.
The ray is transmitted without changing direction.
explanation: Since the ray travels from higher to lower refractive index and i > c, it undergoes total internal reflection.
sourceNote: Original item aligned to IB Physics guide for first assessment 2025, and benchmarked against the supplied C.3 Paper 1A questions.

stem: The refractive index of a transparent solid in air is 1.60. What is the critical angle for light travelling from the solid to air?

stem: Light passes from medium 1, of refractive index n₁, into medium 2, of refractive index n₂. The wavelengths in the media are λ₁ and λ₂ respectively. What is the ratio λ₂/λ₁?
options: n₂/n₁
n₁/n₂
n₁n₂
1/(n₁n₂)
explanation: Frequency is unchanged on refraction and v = c/n. Therefore λ₂/λ₁ = v₂/v₁ = (c/n₂)/(c/n₁) = n₁/n₂.
sourceNote: Original item aligned to IB Physics guide for first assessment 2025, and benchmarked against the supplied C.3 Paper 1A questions.

stem: Two pulses of the same shape and amplitude travel towards each other on a string, one upwards and the other downwards. What happens when they overlap exactly?
options: The pulses are permanently destroyed.
The resultant displacement is zero at that instant; both pulses then continue.
They reflect from each other and reverse direction.
The resultant amplitude doubles.
explanation: The displacements add algebraically and cancel temporarily; superposition does not destroy either pulse.
sourceNote: Original item aligned to IB Physics guide for first assessment 2025, and benchmarked against the supplied C.3 Paper 1A questions.

stem: Two light sources produce a stable interference pattern on a screen. Which condition is necessary?
options: They must have equal intensities at every point.
They must have the same amplitude.
They must emit different frequencies.
They must maintain a constant phase difference.
explanation: Coherent sources have the same frequency and a constant phase difference, enabling stable interference.
sourceNote: Original item aligned to IB Physics guide for first assessment 2025, and benchmarked against the supplied C.3 Paper 1A questions.

stem: Two coherent sources S₁ and S₂ oscillate in phase with a wavelength of 0.080 m. At the point P shown, the distances from the two sources are 2.64 m and 2.40 m. What type of interference occurs at P?
options: Constructive, because the path difference is three wavelengths.
Destructive, because the path difference is half a wavelength.
Destructive, because the path difference is three wavelengths.
Neither, because path differences must be zero.
explanation: Path difference = 0.24 m = 3λ, giving constructive interference for in-phase sources.
diagramAlt: Coherent sources S1 and S2 with distances 2.64 m and 2.40 m to screen point P.
sourceNote: Original item aligned to IB Physics guide for first assessment 2025, and benchmarked against the supplied C.3 Paper 1A questions.

stem: At a point on a screen, waves from two coherent, in-phase sources have a path difference of 3.5λ. What is the interference at this point?
options: Constructive: the waves arrive in phase.
Constructive: the path difference is an integer number of wavelengths.
Destructive: the waves arrive in antiphase.
Destructive: path difference is an even multiple of λ.
explanation: An odd multiple of λ/2 produces a phase difference of an odd multiple of π, giving destructive interference.
sourceNote: Original item aligned to IB Physics guide for first assessment 2025, and benchmarked against the supplied C.3 Paper 1A questions.

stem: At point X, two coherent waves of equal amplitude A meet in phase. The combined amplitude is 2A. How does the resulting intensity compare with the intensity of either wave acting alone?
options: It is unchanged.
It is twice as large.
It is three times as large.
It is four times as large.
explanation: For a given medium, intensity is proportional to amplitude squared, so (2A)²/A² = 4.
sourceNote: Original item aligned to IB Physics guide for first assessment 2025, and benchmarked against the supplied C.3 Paper 1A questions.

stem: A double-slit experiment uses light of wavelength 500 nm. The slits are separated by 0.25 mm and the screen is 1.5 m away. What is the fringe separation?
options: 3.0 mm
30 mm

stem: In a Young double-slit experiment, both the wavelength and slit separation are doubled while the screen distance remains the same. What happens to fringe separation?
options: It is unchanged.
It doubles.
It is halved.
It is four times larger.
explanation: s = λD/d; doubling both λ and d leaves their ratio unchanged.
sourceNote: Original item aligned to IB Physics guide for first assessment 2025, and benchmarked against the supplied C.3 Paper 1A questions.

stem: In a double-slit experiment, a central bright fringe is labelled order zero. A point X is the fourth dark fringe on one side of the central maximum. What is the path difference at X?
options: 2λ
explanation: Dark fringes from the centre occur at λ/2, 3λ/2, 5λ/2, 7λ/2, ...
sourceNote: Original item aligned to IB Physics guide for first assessment 2025, and benchmarked against the supplied C.3 Paper 1A questions.

stem: A monochromatic beam illuminates a narrow rectangular slit. The slit width is halved. What is the approximate change in the angular width of the central diffraction maximum?
options: It is halved.
It doubles.
It remains constant.
It becomes four times larger.
explanation: For small angles, the first minima satisfy θ ≈ λ/b, so the central width 2θ is inversely proportional to slit width.
sourceNote: Original item aligned to IB Physics guide for first assessment 2025, and benchmarked against the supplied C.3 Paper 1A questions.

stem: Monochromatic light illuminates a rectangular slit uniformly. The slit width is increased while the incident intensity per unit area is unchanged. Which change is expected?
options: The central maximum becomes narrower and brighter.
The central maximum becomes wider and brighter.
The central maximum becomes narrower and dimmer.
The central maximum becomes wider and dimmer.
explanation: A wider slit transmits more light and reduces the angular width of the central maximum; on-axis coherent field is greater.
sourceNote: Original item aligned to IB Physics guide for first assessment 2025, and benchmarked against the supplied C.3 Paper 1A questions.

stem: A diffraction grating has 400 lines per millimetre and is illuminated normally by light of wavelength 600 nm. What is the highest observable diffraction order?
explanation: d = 2.5 μm, so m ≤ d/λ = 2.5/0.60 = 4.17. The maximum integer order is 4.
sourceNote: Original item aligned to IB Physics guide for first assessment 2025, and benchmarked against the supplied C.3 Paper 1A questions.

stem: White light is incident normally on a diffraction grating. Which description of the pattern is correct?
options: The central maximum is violet, with red first-order maxima on either side.
The central maximum is red, with violet first-order maxima on either side.
The central maximum is white; in each first-order spectrum violet is closer to the centre than red.
The central maximum is white; in each first-order spectrum red is closer to the centre than violet.
explanation: At m=0 all wavelengths overlap as white. For a fixed order sinθ = mλ/d; red has a larger diffraction angle than violet.
sourceNote: Original item aligned to IB Physics guide for first assessment 2025, and benchmarked against the supplied C.3 Paper 1A questions.

stem: A double-slit pattern has closely spaced bright fringes within a broad single-slit diffraction envelope. If the width of each slit is reduced but the slit separation stays fixed, what happens?
options: The interference fringe spacing increases and the diffraction envelope narrows.
The interference fringe spacing decreases and the diffraction envelope widens.
The interference fringe spacing stays the same and the diffraction envelope narrows.
The interference fringe spacing stays the same and the diffraction envelope widens.
explanation: The fringe spacing depends on slit separation, which is unchanged. Smaller slit width widens the diffraction envelope.
sourceNote: Original item aligned to IB Physics guide for first assessment 2025, and benchmarked against the supplied C.3 Paper 1A questions.

stem: A grating produces second-order maxima at 30° for light of wavelength 450 nm at normal incidence. What is the line density?
options: 2.8 × 10⁵ lines m⁻¹
5.6 × 10⁵ lines m⁻¹
1.1 × 10⁶ lines m⁻¹
2.2 × 10⁶ lines m⁻¹
explanation: d = mλ/sinθ = 2(450 × 10⁻⁹)/0.5 = 1.8 × 10⁻⁶ m. Density = 1/d = 5.6 × 10⁵ lines m⁻¹.
sourceNote: Original item aligned to IB Physics guide for first assessment 2025, and benchmarked against the supplied C.3 Paper 1A questions.
